beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about whether a model's confidence in its own answer actually matches how often that answer is right, and three questions that test whether its stated confidence means anything at all.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: Ask a model how sure it is of an answer, and it'll often tell you, in words, or even a number. The trouble is, that confidence can sound exactly the same whether the model is right or completely wrong. Sounding sure and being right are two different claims.
beats.new_visual_element: Two answer cards, identically confident in tone, one marked correct, one marked wrong -- same stated confidence, opposite outcome

shot.note: Generic/hypothetical scenario -- no real model named, per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test, before any example: three questions. One, bucket the claims: group every answer by how confident it sounds, and check, within each bucket, how often is it actually right? Two, count the cases: one lucky or unlucky answer proves nothing, does the pattern hold across many questions, not just one? Three, spot the bluff: would a genuinely hedged, uncertain answer ever get miscounted as a confident claim? If the buckets don't match reality, it isn't calibrated, it's just confident-sounding.
beats.new_visual_element: Checklist card, all 3 tests shown together (Bucket the Claims / Count the Cases / Spot the Bluff)

shot.note: Framework shown fully before any example, matching prior STEM videos' rubric beat.

beats.narration_text: Here's a documented pattern. Take every answer a model gave at roughly the same stated confidence, say, ninety percent sure, across many different questions, and bucket them together. Count how many were actually correct. If that bucket is only right sixty percent of the time, the model's confidence number isn't tracking its real accuracy. It's overconfident, and the gap shows up no matter which question in the bucket you check.
beats.new_visual_element: A '90% confident' bucket of answer chips, a stated-confidence bar next to an actual-accuracy bar, the gap between them highlighted

shot.note: [Source: FACTCHECK.md #2 -- generic illustration of a documented pattern, no real model named] Both bars must be visible together so the gap reads without narration alone.

beats.narration_text: Now the case that would break this test if it were sloppy. Take a model that hedges on genuinely hard questions and sounds confident only on the easy ones. Bucket its ninety-percent confident answers the same way. This time, the actual accuracy in that bucket is also close to ninety percent. Same bucket, same test, a completely different, and genuinely well-calibrated, result.
beats.new_visual_element: The same bucket-and-bars layout, this time the bars nearly match -- a checkmark where B04 had a gap

shot.note: Stress-tests the framework against a naive 'any confident answer is overconfident' over-trigger. Visually distinct resolution from B04 (matching bars vs a gap).

beats.narration_text: Here's something to try today. Ask a model several factual questions you already know the answers to, and have it state a confidence number for each one. Group the answers by that number. Check, in each group, what fraction were actually correct? If a ninety-percent-confident group is only right half the time, you've just measured a real calibration gap.
beats.new_visual_element: The 3 tests restated as a checklist card

shot.note: Concrete action, not a restatement of B03 -- should read as a checklist/task card, not another copy of the framework card.

beats.narration_text: Sounding sure and being right are different claims. The only way to know if a model's confidence means anything is to check whether it tracks real accuracy across many cases, not just one.
